opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, part of it is just a question of comparative advantage. I was trained as a physicist, so people naturally assume that if I'm working in AI, the most natural thing would be to go back and apply it to physics: use models to do theoretical calculations, find new results, that kind of thing. And I think that's a wonderful direction. But I feel the most important bottleneck right now isn't really on the physics side. It's on the side of making the models themselves more capable.

If you think about it, whatever a model can do for physics, for math, for biology, is downstream of how good the general model is. If I spend my time building a specialized pipeline for, say, some problem in high-energy theory, maybe I get a nice paper out of it. But a year later the next generation of general models might just do that out of the box. So the leverage feels much higher working on the core capabilities: reasoning, long-horizon tasks, things like that.

There's also a more personal reason. When I left physics, part of me felt I had kind of reached a point where I wasn't sure my own contribution there was going to be that distinctive. Coming back to it through AI risks being a bit nostalgic rather than strategic. And there are a lot of very smart people, including many physicists I know, who are excited to use these tools in their own fields. They understand their problems much better than I do now. I'd rather they do that and I help make the tools good enough that it actually works.

So it's not that I don't care about AI for physics. I actually think it will be one of the most exciting things to happen in the next few years. I just think my time is better spent a bit further upstream for now. Maybe later, when the models are strong enough, I'll come back and have some fun with it.

r001.rationale: He says he is unsure his contribution in physics would be distinctive and that physicists know their problems better, but does not clearly state that his participation would make little difference to the work already underway.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it comes down to where I think my own marginal value is right now.

AI for physics is a wonderful direction, and I'm quite sure it will happen. But if you look at what actually gates it, it isn't a shortage of physicists who understand the problems. It's the capability of the models themselves. A model that can't yet carry a long chain of rigorous reasoning without drifting, or that can't tell when it's confused, is not going to discover new physics no matter how carefully a physicist curates the dataset or designs the benchmark. So the bottleneck sits upstream, in making the models fundamentally smarter and more reliable. That's where I want to spend my time.

There's also a more personal reason. I spent a decade doing condensed matter and quantum many-body theory, and I loved it. If I went into "AI for physics" right now, I think I would end up doing physics with AI as a tool, because that's the habit my brain has. I would be the physicist in the room, not the person learning how these systems actually work. I came here to understand intelligence from the inside, and that requires me to be a bit uncomfortable, to be a beginner again on the core problems.

And frankly, there are many excellent people already working on applying AI to science, and they'll do it better than I would at this moment. When the models cross a certain threshold, the physics applications will come very quickly, almost on their own. I'd rather help push toward that threshold, and then maybe come back to physics later with a much more powerful collaborator. So it's not that I'm leaving physics behind. I'm taking a detour that I think leads back to it faster.

r001.rationale: He says many excellent people are already applying AI to science and “they’ll do it better than I would at this moment,” communicating that his participation would add little to the work already underway.

astra-6.text:
For now, I think it’s a question of comparative advantage. Using AI for physics requires a good understanding of which physics problems matter and where existing methods fall short. I don’t think I have enough of that expertise to judge those questions well, so I’d rather leave them to people who do.

My own interest is more in how to make AI systems broadly capable—how they reason, interact with an environment, and accomplish tasks. If we make progress there, those capabilities could also become useful tools for people working on physics.

r001.rationale: The response says he lacks expertise to judge which physics problems matter and would leave that work to others. It does not state that his own participation would make little difference to work already underway.

sol-6.1.text: For me, it’s mainly a question of where I can contribute most. I’m more interested in how to build AI systems that can reason, act, and solve problems in a general way. Applying those systems to physics requires deep domain knowledge, and there are people much better positioned to do that. So for now, I’d rather focus on improving the general capabilities and leave the physics applications to people who really understand the problems.

r001.rationale: The response says others are better positioned to apply AI to physics, but does not state that Shunyu Yao’s own participation would make little difference to the work already underway.
